verses.text: Solomon the son of David was firmly established in his kingdom, and Yahweh  his God  was with him, and made him exceedingly great.
Solomon spoke to all Israel, to the captains of thousands and of hundreds, to the judges, and to every prince in all Israel, the heads of the fathers’ households.
So Solomon, and all the assembly with him, went to the high place that was at Gibeon; for God’s Tent of Meeting was there, which Yahweh’s servant Moses had made in the wilderness.
But David had brought God’s ark up from Kiriath Jearim to the place that David had prepared for it; for he had pitched a tent for it at Jerusalem.
Moreover the bronze altar that Bezalel the son of Uri, the son of Hur, had made was there before Yahweh’s tabernacle; and Solomon and the assembly were seeking counsel there.
Solomon went up there to the bronze altar before Yahweh, which was at the Tent of Meeting, and offered one thousand burnt offerings on it.
That night, God appeared to Solomon and said to him, “Ask for what you want me to give you.”
Solomon said to God, “You have shown great loving kindness to David my father, and have made me king in his place.
Now, Yahweh God, let your promise to David my father be established; for you have made me king over a people like the dust of the earth in multitude.
Now give me wisdom and knowledge, that I may go out and come in before this people; for who can judge this great people of yours?”

God said to Solomon, “Because this was in your heart, and you have not asked riches, wealth, honor, or the life of those who hate you, nor yet have you asked for long life; but have asked for wisdom and knowledge for yourself, that you may judge my people, over whom I have made you king,
therefore wisdom and knowledge is granted to you. I will give you riches, wealth, and honor, such as none of the kings have had who have been before you had, and none after you will have.”
So Solomon came from the high place that was at Gibeon, from before the Tent of Meeting, to Jerusalem; and he reigned over Israel.
Solomon gathered chariots and horsemen. He had one thousand four hundred chariots and twelve thousand horsemen that he placed in the chariot cities, and with the king at Jerusalem.
The king made silver and gold to be as common as stones in Jerusalem, and he made cedars to be as common as the sycamore trees that are in the lowland.
The horses which Solomon had were brought out of Egypt and from Kue. The king’s merchants purchased them from Kue.
They brought up and brought out of Egypt a chariot for six hundred pieces of silver, and a horse for one hundred fifty.  They also exported them to the Hittite kings and the Syrian  kings.

footnotes.content: Solomon is firm in his kingdom—not because he schemes or grasps, but because the Lord's hand is with him. The strength a young man needs comes not from his own nerve, but from knowing he stands under the blessing of the Almighty. Notice: it's Yahweh who makes him great.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Solomon gathers the leaders—thousands and hundreds, judges and princes. A king who listens to counsel from every rank of his people shows wisdom before he asks for it. He knows that a kingdom stands on the strength of many voices, not one voice alone.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: To Gibeon they go—the high place where God's Tent of Meeting still stands. Before seeking a crown's wisdom, Solomon seeks the place of God's presence. The Tent, made by Moses in the wilderness, reminds us that meeting the Lord there is older than any kingdom.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: David had brought the ark to Jerusalem—a city, not the wilderness. The ark is God's throne on earth. Even as the Tent remains at Gibeon, the ark's presence in Jerusalem shows that the Lord dwells at the heart of the kingdom. Two places, one God.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Bezalel the craftsman—his bronze altar still stands before the Tent. How the Lord endows the gifted hand to serve Him! An altar made long ago in the wilderness, now bearing Solomon's seeking. The work of faithful hands outlasts the generation that made it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: One thousand burnt offerings—a staggering number, a lavish gift. Solomon gives not from habit, but from a heart overflowing. Before he asks, he gives. This is the rhythm of grace: the one who has received much pours it out without measure.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: That night, God appears. Not in thunder from Mount Sinai, but in the quiet of darkness—a dream-vision to a young king who has just sacrificed a thousand offerings. The Lord draws near to those who draw near to Him, whispering an invitation: Ask.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Solomon speaks of David's kindness—his father's record. He knows his throne is not his own making. Humility is remembering that you inherit grace from those before you, and that the Lord is the Giver of all.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Dust of the earth in multitude—Israel's people are countless, overwhelming in their number. A young king feels the weight of the promise given to Abraham. The task is too great; only God's faithfulness can uphold such a people.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Solomon asks for wisdom and knowledge to judge well. Not for power over enemies, not for long life or riches—but to lead justly. A king's true strength is not in his sword, but in a mind that seeks what is right for his people.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: God sees what was in his heart. Solomon did not ask for riches, life, or the ruin of enemies—he asked for wisdom. The test is passed not by speaking the right words, but by desiring the right thing. The Lord reads desires, not speeches.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Wisdom and knowledge are given, yes—and riches and honor besides. The Lord does not withhold good things from those who seek Him first. He heaps blessing on a heart that prizes His wisdom above all earthly gain.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: From Gibeon to Jerusalem—from the high place of the Tent to the city where the ark dwells—Solomon returns as a different man. Something has happened in the dark; he carries it back into daylight.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Chariots and horsemen gathered—twelve thousand soldiers mounted and ready. The promise blooms into reality. A king reigns not by spirit alone, but by the strength of his armies. Watch what a man does with the gifts that flow in.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Silver and gold 'as common as stones,' cedar 'as common as sycamore in the lowland.' The wealth is staggering, beyond measure. Abundance can be a test as much as scarcity. Will he remember who gave it?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Horses brought from Egypt, merchants dealing the trade—the machinery of commerce and power turns. The gifts God gives are real, but they move through the hands of men, and men can forget.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Chariots and horses exported to the Hittite kings and Syrian kings—Solomon's wealth flows outward, binding him to the nations. Readers today hear an echo: when we prosper, we grow entangled with the world's systems. The question returns: do we remember who gave us the wisdom to begin with?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
